## Supplementary Material to "DStressR enables statistical analysis and inference of large-scale arrayed chemical genomics screens" {.unnumbered}

### Supplementary Note A: Software Implementation {.unnumbered}

DStressR is implemented as an R package for reproducible analysis of arrayed
promoter-reporter screens. The exported workflow follows the statistical
layers described in the main text. `prepare_assay()` standardizes a
long-format assay table, constructs the response, records the reference
condition, and stores the technical design. Growth exponents can be estimated,
supplied, or fixed, with a dedicated set of control-well covariates if this
should differ from the downstream model design. Matched background reporters
can be calibrated by Huber regression, ordinary least squares, or direct
subtraction. Numeric design variables such as concentration index can be
retained as quantitative covariates, while plate, batch, and replicate labels
can be handled as factors.

`fit_destress()` fits the model-based workflow and stores response metadata,
growth-exponent estimates, background-calibration estimates, model settings,
reporter-perturbation effects, p-values, and adjusted p-values. Results are
exported with `results()`, inspected with `model_parameters()`, and converted
into directional hit calls with `call_hits()`. We use the model-based workflow
as the default path, while median-polish and Salmonella empty-vector-control
presets reproduce published screen-specific analyses and enable comparison
with the model-based estimand.

The software flow mirrors the statistical construction in the paper. First, a
long-format screen is mapped to an assay object with explicit columns for the
reporter signal, the growth signal, the reporter, the perturbation variable, the
reference condition, and technical covariates. The names of these columns remain
dataset-specific. In the Binsfeld screen, the perturbation column is the original
`drug` label; in the Dash fluorescence experiment, it is a derived `stress`
label. Second, the response scale is constructed from the reporter and growth
summaries, optionally using an estimated reporter-specific growth exponent and
an empty-vector or other background reporter. Third, the model-based analysis
estimates reporter-perturbation effects, applies the selected uncertainty model,
adjusts p-values within the chosen family, and returns directional calls.
Finally, the same result table is used for visualization, comparison with dedicated
analyses, and manuscript-scale exports.

For a generic arrayed reporter screen without a matched background reporter,
the complete model-based workflow can be written as:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(DStressR)

assay <- prepare_assay(
  screen_table,
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "perturbation",
  control = "DMSO",
  lux = "lux_auc",
  growth = "od_fixed_time",
  growth_exponent = "estimate",
  batch = "plate",
  replicate = "replicate"
)

fit <- fit_destress(
  assay,
  preset = "model",
  technical = c("plate", "replicate"),
  empirical_bayes = TRUE,
  adjustment = "by_reporter"
)

pair_results <- results(fit)
hits <- call_hits(pair_results, fdr = 0.05, effect = "specific_effect")
```

When a matched empty-vector or background reporter is available, it enters
during response construction:

```{r}
#| eval: false
assay_evc <- prepare_assay(
  screen_table,
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "perturbation",
  control = "DMSO",
  lux = "lux_auc",
  growth = "od_fixed_time",
  growth_exponent = "estimate",
  batch = "plate",
  replicate = "replicate",
  background_reporter = "EVC",
  background_method = "huber",
  background_by = c("perturbation", "plate", "replicate")
)

fit_evc <- fit_destress(
  assay_evc,
  preset = "model",
  technical = c("plate", "replicate"),
  empirical_bayes = TRUE,
  adjustment = "by_reporter"
)
```

For the public Binsfeld data object, the source-faithful perturbation variable is
`drug`. The two water controls are supplied together and are pooled internally as
the model reference without modifying the original input column:

```{r}
#| eval: false
binsfeld_assay <- prepare_assay(
  binsfeld_reporter_auc,
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "drug",
  control = c("Water_1", "Water_2"),
  lux = "lux_auc",
  growth = "od_auc",
  growth_exponent = "estimate",
  batch = "dose_level",
  replicate = "replicate",
  growth_covariates = "replicate",
  numeric_covariates = "dose_level",
  background_reporter = "EVC",
  background_method = "huber",
  background_by = c("drug", "dose_level", "replicate")
)
```

For the Dash fluorescence/OD example, the local workflow converts the
weak-stress condition into a `stress` column and analyzes reporter-window units:

```{r}
#| eval: false
dash_assay <- prepare_assay(
  dash_weak_stress,
  reporter = "pseudo_reporter",
  perturbation = "stress",
  control = "Standard",
  lux = "gfp_auc",
  growth = "od_auc",
  growth_exponent = stress_alpha,
  replicate = "replicate"
)
```

The fitted object retains the model settings and intermediate quantities used
in the statistical analysis:

```{r}
#| eval: false
model_parameters(fit_evc)
head(results(fit_evc))

plot_volcano(
  results(fit_evc),
  effect = "specific_effect",
  padj = "specific_padj_by_reporter"
)

plot_response_heatmap(
  results(fit_evc),
  value = "specific_effect"
)
```

Optional model extensions use the same assay object and change only the
modeling layer. For example, a low-rank background adjustment or a full
promoter-by-compound interaction model can be requested explicitly:

```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_low_rank <- fit_destress(
  assay_evc,
  preset = "model",
  technical = c("plate", "replicate"),
  empirical_bayes = TRUE,
  background_rank = 1
)

fit_interaction <- fit_destress(
  assay_evc,
  preset = "model",
  technical = c("plate", "replicate"),
  empirical_bayes = TRUE,
  interaction = TRUE
)
```

For CRAN readiness, raw-data preparation and manuscript-scale analyses are kept
outside the installed package. The package ships compact, documented public
data derived from the published *E. coli* promoter-compound screen
[@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol], together with vignettes and tests that exercise the
exported workflow. Full application scripts remain in the source repository so
that the manuscript analyses can be rerun without increasing the installed
package footprint.

\clearpage

### Supplementary Note B: Dedicated Estimator Definitions {.unnumbered}

The package also retains two project-level estimators for reproducibility of
published screen-specific analyses: a median-polish estimator and a Salmonella
empty-vector-control estimator. Both start from pre-normalized reporter responses, construct
replicate-level z-test p-values from DMSO or other reference wells, aggregate
replicate evidence conservatively at the promoter-compound level, and adjust
p-values within promoter. These estimators reproduce earlier screen-specific
workflows; the main statistical framework uses the model-based target defined
in Section 2.

### B.1 Median-Polish Workflow {.unnumbered}

The median-polish estimator follows the Campylobacter reporter-screen workflow
of @Zannoni2026CampylobacterDrugScreen. It starts from a pre-normalized response
$u_{hk}$, where $h$ denotes a promoter-library-plate-replicate group and $k$
denotes a compound or control well. In that workflow, $u_{hk}$ is the
growth-normalized luminescence summary on the log scale. If $\mathcal d_h$ is
the set of DMSO wells in group $h$, the DMSO-centered response is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:median-polish-dmso-centering}
m_{hk}
  =
  u_{hk}
  -
  \frac{1}{|\mathcal{d}_h|}
  \sum_{k' \in \mathcal{d}_h} u_{hk'} .
\end{equation}

Median polish decomposes the group-by-compound matrix as

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:median-polish-decomposition}
m_{hk}
  =
  \eta^{\mathrm{mp}}
  +
  \rho_h^{\mathrm{mp}}
  +
  \kappa_k^{\mathrm{mp}}
  +
  \varepsilon_{hk}^{\mathrm{mp}},
\end{equation}

where $\varepsilon_{hk}^{\mathrm{mp}}$ is the residual used for testing. Within each
group, the DMSO residuals define the Gaussian null used for the z test,
with $\bar\varepsilon_{h\mathcal{d}}^{\mathrm{mp}}$ and
$s_{h\mathcal{d}}^{\mathrm{mp}}$ denoting the mean and standard deviation of
$\varepsilon_{hk}^{\mathrm{mp}}$ over $k\in\mathcal d_h$:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:median-polish-null}
\begin{aligned}
T_{hk}^{\mathrm{mp}}
  &=
  \frac{\varepsilon_{hk}^{\mathrm{mp}} - \bar\varepsilon_{h\mathcal{d}}^{\mathrm{mp}}}
       {s_{h\mathcal{d}}^{\mathrm{mp}}},\\
\pi_{hk}
  &=
  2\,\Pr\{Z \ge |T_{hk}^{\mathrm{mp}}|\},
  \qquad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Mapping each group $h$ back to promoter $a$ and replicate context $t$ gives
replicate-level p-values $\pi_{ajt}$. For each promoter-compound pair, DStressR
keeps the conservative aggregate

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:median-polish-pvalue-aggregation}
\pi_{aj}^{\mathrm{pair}}
  =
  \max_t \pi_{ajt},
\end{equation}

followed by Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment within promoter. The normality of
the DMSO-centered null values can be assessed with the Lilliefors test
[@Lilliefors1967].

In the R package, the workflow can be called either directly or through the
dedicated preset:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Direct dedicated estimator
mp_fit <- fit_median_polish(
  screen_table,
  response = "response",
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "perturbation",
  control = c("DMSO1", "DMSO2"),
  replicate = "replicate"
)

# Equivalent preset interface
mp_fit <- fit_destress(
  screen_table,
  preset = "median_polish",
  response = "response",
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "perturbation",
  control = c("DMSO1", "DMSO2"),
  replicate = "replicate"
)
```

### B.2 Salmonella Empty-Vector-Control Workflow {.unnumbered}

The Salmonella empty-vector-control estimator follows the Salmonella
reporter-screen workflow of @Amstalden2026SalmonellaStressScreen.
It starts from a pre-normalized, median-centered reporter response $u_{ajt}$,
where $t$ indexes replicate observations, and uses a reporter strain without
promoter insert, denoted $e$, to estimate compound-specific reporter
background. For compound $j$, let $\mathcal r_e(j)$ denote the retained
empty-vector replicate observations. The empty-vector baseline is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:empty-vector-baseline}
\bar u_{ej}
  =
  \frac{1}{|\mathcal r_e(j)|}
  \sum_{t \in \mathcal r_e(j)} u_{ejt}.
\end{equation}

Each reporter observation is transformed to an empty-vector fold change,
$q_{ajt}=u_{ajt}-\bar u_{ej}$.

DMSO values within promoter-replicate strata define the null. Here
$\bar q_{a0t}$ and $s_{a0t}$ denote the mean and standard deviation of the
empty-vector-adjusted DMSO values for promoter $a$ and replicate stratum $t$:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:empty-vector-null}
\begin{aligned}
T_{ajt}^{\mathrm{evc}}
  &=
  \frac{q_{ajt} - \bar q_{a0t}}
       {s_{a0t}},\\
\pi_{ajt}
  &=
  2\,\Pr\{Z \ge |T_{ajt}^{\mathrm{evc}}|\},
  \qquad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

As in the median-polish estimator, DStressR keeps the largest replicate-level
p-value for each promoter-compound pair and applies within-promoter
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. The DMSO empty-vector-adjusted values within
each promoter-replicate stratum can again be assessed with the Lilliefors test
[@Lilliefors1967].

In the R package, the workflow can again be called directly or through the
dedicated preset:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Direct dedicated estimator
evc_fit <- fit_empty_vector_control(
  screen_table,
  response = "response",
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "perturbation",
  empty_vector_reporter = "EVC",
  control = c("DMSO1", "DMSO2"),
  replicate = "replicate"
)

# Equivalent preset interface
evc_fit <- fit_destress(
  screen_table,
  preset = "evc",
  response = "response",
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "perturbation",
  empty_vector_reporter = "EVC",
  control = c("DMSO1", "DMSO2"),
  replicate = "replicate"
)
```

\clearpage

### Supplementary Note C: Empirical-Bayes Variance Moderation {.unnumbered}

This supplementary note gives the moment calculation used for the prior degrees of
freedom in the moderated test. The model is the scaled inverse-$\chi^2$
empirical-Bayes variance model underlying moderated $t$ tests in `limma`
[@Smyth2004limmaEB; @Ritchie2015limma]. Let $v_\omega$ denote the raw
model-based variance for tested contrast $\omega$, and let $\nu_\omega$ denote
the residual degrees of freedom used for the ordinary $t$ statistic. DStressR
uses

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-sampling-model}
v_\omega \mid \sigma_\omega^2
  \sim
  \sigma_\omega^2 \frac{\chi^2_{\nu_\omega}}{\nu_\omega},
\qquad
\sigma_\omega^2
  \sim
  s_0^2 \frac{\nu_0}{\chi^2_{\nu_0}}.
\end{equation}

For estimating the empirical prior by moments, DStressR uses a representative
degree of freedom $\nu_\star$ from the tested contrasts, currently
$\nu_\star=\operatorname{median}_{\omega}\{\nu_\omega:
\nu_\omega \text{ finite and } \nu_\omega>0\}$.

This approximation is exact for balanced designs and avoids letting a small
number of sparse reporter-wise fits determine the empirical-Bayes prior. With
this representative degree of freedom, the marginal variance estimate follows
approximately $v_\omega\sim s_0^2 F_{\nu_\star,\nu_0}$.

On the logarithmic scale, the first two moments are

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-log-mean}
\mathbb E\{\log v_\omega\}
  =
\log s_0^2
  +
  \psi(\nu_\star/2)-\log(\nu_\star/2)
  -
  \psi(\nu_0/2)+\log(\nu_0/2),
\end{equation}

and

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-log-variance}
\operatorname{Var}\{\log v_\omega\}
  =
  \psi_1(\nu_\star/2)+\psi_1(\nu_0/2),
\end{equation}

where $\psi$ is the digamma function and $\psi_1$ is the trigamma function.
Writing $\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}\{\log v_\omega\}$ for the empirical
variance of finite positive log-variance estimates, the prior degrees of
freedom are estimated by

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-prior-df}
\widehat{\nu}_0
  =
  2\,
  \psi_1^{-1}
  \left[
    \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}\{\log v_\omega\}
    -
    \psi_1(\nu_\star/2)
  \right],
\end{equation}

with a large prior-degree cap when the empirical excess variance is
non-positive. Given $\widehat{\nu}_0$, the prior variance is estimated as

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-prior-variance}
\log \widehat{s}_0^2
  =
  \overline{\log v_\omega}
  -
  \psi(\nu_\star/2)+\log(\nu_\star/2)
  +
  \psi(\widehat{\nu}_0/2)-\log(\widehat{\nu}_0/2).
\end{equation}

The moderated variance and moderated statistic are then

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-moderated-statistic}
\widetilde v_\omega
  =
  \frac{\nu_\omega v_\omega+\widehat{\nu}_0\widehat{s}_0^2}
       {\nu_\omega+\widehat{\nu}_0},
\qquad
\widetilde t_\omega
  =
  \frac{\widehat{\Delta}_\omega}{\sqrt{\widetilde v_\omega}},
\end{equation}

and the moderated p-value is evaluated against a
$t_{\nu_\omega+\widehat{\nu}_0}$ reference distribution.

```{r}
  x <- gsub("Binsfeld reference", "Ref", x, fixed = TRUE)

  x <- gsub("DStressR with EV control", "EVC", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("DStressR without EVC", "No-EVC", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("DStressR with EVC", "EVC", x, fixed = TRUE)

  x
}

)]

)

  union_tbl[order(union_tbl$Prom., union_tbl$Cmpd.), ],

  longtable = knitr::is_latex_output()
)
```

### Supplementary Note E: E. coli DStressR Analysis with the Full Interaction Model {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
interaction_dir <- file.path("..", "..", "analysis", "outputs", "ecoli_interaction_model")
interaction_dims <- rbind(
  read.delim(file.path(interaction_dir, "interaction_without_ev_model_matrix.tsv")),
  read.delim(file.path(interaction_dir, "interaction_with_ev_model_matrix.tsv"))
)
interaction_dims$response_modeling <- ifelse(
  grepl("_with_ev$", interaction_dims$analysis),
  "with EVC",
  "without EVC"
)
interaction_dims$inference <- ifelse(
  interaction_dims$model == "interaction",
  "interaction",
  "additive"
)
interaction_dims <- interaction_dims[, c(
  "response_modeling", "inference", "n_observations",
  "n_coefficients", "residual_df", "sigma"
)]
interaction_dims$sigma <- signif(interaction_dims$sigma, digits = 3)
names(interaction_dims) <- c(
  "Response modeling", "Inference", "N", "Coefficients", "Residual df", "Sigma"
)
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  cat("\\begin{table}[H]\n")
  cat("\\caption{Design-matrix dimensions for the additive and full interaction models fitted to the WT \\textit{E. coli} screen.}\n")
  cat("\\centering\\begingroup\\small\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{4pt}\n")
}
cat(knitr::kable(
  interaction_dims,
  format = if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "latex" else "pipe",
  booktabs = knitr::is_latex_output()
), sep = "\n")
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  cat("\n\\endgroup\\end{table}\n")
}
```

The WT *E. coli* screen was small enough to fit the optional full
promoter-by-compound interaction model described in Section 2.4.
This is a downstream testing model for the already constructed DStressR
response. The tested grid
contains 7 non-empty-vector promoters and 94 non-water compounds, yielding 658
tested promoter-compound pairs. Water is the reference condition. With
treatment coding, $a_i$ denotes the tested promoter for observation $i$, $j_i$
denotes one of the 95 condition levels including Water, $\lambda_{a_i}\in
\mathbb{R}^{6}$ is the promoter indicator vector, $\kappa_{j_i}\in
\mathbb{R}^{94}$ is the non-water condition indicator vector, and
$x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ contains the technical covariates replicate and dose
level. Let
$\widehat y_i$ denote the final response after growth-response modeling and,
for the EVC workflow, EVC calibration. The concrete full interaction model
fitted in this supplementary note is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-ecoli-interaction-model-concrete}
\widehat y_i =
\beta_0
+ \lambda_{a_i}^{\top}\beta
+ \kappa_{j_i}^{\top}\theta
+ x_i^{\top}\zeta
+ (\lambda_{a_i}\otimes \kappa_{j_i})^{\top}\phi
+ \varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal N(0,\sigma^2),
\end{equation}

where $\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{6}$, $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{94}$,
$\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$, and $\phi\in\mathbb{R}^{564}$ contains the optional
promoter-by-compound interaction coefficients. Thus, the fitted interaction
model has $1 + 6 + 94 + 2 + (6 \times 94) = 667$ coefficients. The
corresponding additive model omits $\phi$ and therefore has 103 coefficients.
The uncalibrated interaction run uses $M=5148$ observations.
The empty-vector-calibrated interaction run uses $M=5127$ observations after
response-level calibration and removal of the empty-vector reporter from the
tested promoter set. Both runs use moderated $t$ tests, within-promoter
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment, and FDR 0.05 for hit calling.

The Venn-style panel shows the five compared hit sets, with numbers placed directly on the corresponding non-empty intersections. The central overlap contains 28 pairs called by all five analyses.](../../analysis/outputs/ecoli_interaction_model/interaction_joint_venn_plot.png){#fig-appendix-ecoli-interaction-hit-overlap width="100%" fig-align="center"}

```{r}
key_pairs <- key_pairs[, c(
  "promoter", "compound", "binsfeld_hit", "modeled_hit",
  "evc_huber_hit", "interaction_without_ev_hit", "interaction_with_ev_hit",
  "modeled_effect", "evc_huber_effect",
  "interaction_without_ev_effect", "interaction_with_ev_effect",

  "interaction_with_ev_padj_by_reporter"
)]
hit_code <- function(ref, no_evc, evc, int_no_evc, int_evc) {
  hits <- c(
    if (isTRUE(ref)) "Ref",
    if (isTRUE(no_evc)) "NoE",
    if (isTRUE(evc)) "EVC",
    if (isTRUE(int_no_evc)) "IntN",
    if (isTRUE(int_evc)) "IntE"
  )
  if (length(hits) == 0) "--" else paste(hits, collapse = ",")
}
key_pairs$hit_sets <- mapply(
  hit_code,
  key_pairs$binsfeld_hit,
  key_pairs$modeled_hit,
  key_pairs$evc_huber_hit,
  key_pairs$interaction_without_ev_hit,
  key_pairs$interaction_with_ev_hit,
  USE.NAMES = FALSE
)
key_pairs <- key_pairs[, c(
  "promoter", "compound", "hit_sets",
  "modeled_effect", "evc_huber_effect",
  "interaction_without_ev_effect", "interaction_with_ev_effect",
  "modeled_padj_by_reporter", "evc_huber_padj_by_reporter",
  "interaction_without_ev_padj_by_reporter",
  "interaction_with_ev_padj_by_reporter"
)]
names(key_pairs) <- c(
  "Prom.", "Cmpd.", "Hits",
  "NoE eff.", "EVC eff.", "IntN eff.", "IntE eff.",
  "NoE q", "EVC q", "IntN q", "IntE q"
)
numeric_columns <- vapply(key_pairs, is.numeric, logical(1))
key_pairs[numeric_columns] <- lapply(key_pairs[numeric_columns], signif, digits = 3)
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  cat("\\begingroup\\tiny\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{1.2pt}\\resizebox{\\linewidth}{!}{%\n")
}
cat(knitr::kable(
  key_pairs,
  format = if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "latex" else "pipe",
  booktabs = knitr::is_latex_output()
), sep = "\n")
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  cat("\n}\\endgroup\n")
}
```

### Supplementary Note F: Moderation Diagnostic for the PFIbox Reanalysis {.unnumbered}

The PFIbox reanalysis in the main text uses empirical-Bayes moderated
standard errors for the centered treatment effects. To inspect the contribution
of this layer, we refitted the same treatment-level model from
Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-linear-model} and evaluated the same centered contrasts
with ordinary, unmoderated standard errors. The ordinary test produced a
slightly heavier small-p-value tail and 5,285 reporter-wise FDR calls,
compared with 5,103 calls under variance moderation.

![Moderation diagnostic for the PFIbox promoter-activity screen. The panels compare ordinary t-test and empirical-Bayes moderated raw p-value distributions for the same treatment-level DStressR model in Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-linear-model}. Blue bars mark reporter-wise FDR calls from the centered effects in Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-specific-effect}.](../../analysis/outputs/french_pfibox/promoter_activity_subset/pfibox_pa_moderation_diagnostic_pvalue_histograms.pdf){#fig-appendix-pfibox-moderation-diagnostic width="85%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

### Supplementary Note G: Additional Use Cases {.unnumbered}

#### G.1 Analysis of an E. coli Promoter-Activity Scaling Compendium {.unnumbered}

##### Supplied Summary Data and Response Matrix {.unnumbered}

We next revisited the promoter-activity compendium of Kochanowski et al.
[@Kochanowski2017PromoterScaling], which measured central-metabolism promoter
activities across environmental and metabolic conditions. The public
supplementary tables used here provide processed promoter activities and their
reported standard deviations. We analyze the data as a summary-level response
matrix and use DStressR to recover and extend a published
matrix-decomposition result from summarized reporter data.

Let $n=64$ denote the number of promoters and let $p=25$ denote the number of
conditions. For promoter $a\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and condition
$j\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$, the available data are the processed promoter activity
$A_{aj}>0$, its reported standard deviation $S_{aj}>0$, and the
condition-specific growth rate $\mu_j$. Thus, the supplied data are
$A\in\mathbb R_+^{64\times25}$, $S\in\mathbb R_+^{64\times25}$, and
$\mu\in\mathbb R^{25}$. The glucose condition is the reference condition
$j=0$. We use the supplied promoter activity on the log scale, $x_{aj}=\log_2(A_{aj})$, with approximate response variance $v_{aj}\approx S_{aj}^2/\{A_{aj}^2(\log 2)^2\}$ from the delta method. The DStressR total effect for condition $j$ is the glucose-relative promoter activity change,

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:kochanowski-total-effect}
\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  =
  x_{aj}-x_{a0},
  \qquad j=1,\ldots,p-1.
\end{equation}

The resulting total-effect matrix $T=\{\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}\}\in\mathbb R^{64\times24}$ from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-total-effect} contains one row per promoter and one non-reference condition per column. This matrix is the primary object of analysis in this section.

##### Total, Specific, and Rank-1 Adjusted Effect Estimation {.unnumbered}

As in the preceding sections, DStressR also defines a centered specific effect
by subtracting the condition-wide average total effect across promoters:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:kochanowski-specific-effect}
\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec}}
  =
  \widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}},
  \qquad
  \widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  =
  \frac{1}{64}
  \sum_{a=1}^{64}
  \widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}.
\end{equation}

This contrast asks which promoters deviate from the average response to a
condition. The Kochanowski compendium also has a biologically meaningful
condition-level structure, so we inspect the total-effect matrix before and
after low-rank adjustment.

Kochanowski et al. showed that the promoter-activity matrix is dominated by a
global condition axis related to growth-rate-dependent regulation, with
condition-specific deviations for selected promoters. We fit the summary-level
workflow with glucose as reference and decomposed the total-effect matrix from
Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-total-effect} into a rank-1 background component and
a residual total-effect matrix. Specifically, for the non-reference total-effect matrix $T$, we compute the rank-1 approximation $\widehat B^{(1)}=\widehat d_1\,\widehat u_1\widehat v_1^\top$, where $\widehat d_1$ is the leading singular value and $\widehat u_1\in\mathbb R^{64}$ and $\widehat v_1\in\mathbb R^{24}$ are the corresponding left and right singular vectors. The rank-adjusted total effect is $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},1}=\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}-\widehat B^{(1)}_{aj}$. The rank-1 DStressR perturbation score closely reproduces the first singular
vector reported by Kochanowski et al. After sign alignment, the Pearson
correlation is 0.998 and the Spearman correlation is 0.97. The same score is
also associated with growth rate (Pearson correlation 0.75, Spearman
correlation 0.88). Thus, the DStressR total-effect matrix recovers the known
global promoter-activity axis and yields a residual matrix of
condition-specific deviations (@fig-kochanowski-effect-decomposition).

![DStressR analysis of the Kochanowski promoter-activity compendium. The panels show glucose-relative total effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-total-effect}, the rank-1 component $\widehat B^{(1)}=\widehat d_1\widehat u_1\widehat v_1^\top$, rank-adjusted total effects $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},1}$, the condition-level rank-variance diagnostic, and the comparison between the DStressR rank-1 perturbation score and the first singular-vector axis reported by Kochanowski et al. The sign of the DStressR singular vector is arbitrary and was flipped for comparison.](../../analysis/outputs/kochanowski_promoter_scaling/kochanowski_dstressr_composite_figure.png){#fig-kochanowski-effect-decomposition width="100%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

##### Approximate Summary-Level Inference Results {.unnumbered}

The supplied standard deviations allow an approximate summary-level uncertainty
calculation for the processed promoter activities. For any effect target
$\widehat\theta_{aj}$ with approximate variance $\widehat V_{aj}$, we form the
normal statistic

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:kochanowski-approx-test}
Z_{aj}^{\star}
  =
  \frac{\widehat\theta_{aj}}{\sqrt{\widehat V_{aj}}},
  \qquad
\pi_{aj}^{\star}
  =
  2\,\Pr\{Z\ge |Z_{aj}^{\star}|\},
  \quad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
\end{equation}

We use the approximate p-values from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-approx-test} as an exploratory ranking of reporter-condition pairs under three targets: total effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-total-effect}, centered specific effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-specific-effect}, and rank-adjusted total effects $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},1}$ (@fig-kochanowski-approx-volcano). The volcano
plots summarize the processed compendium with variance-aware scores. Total and
specific effects produce many small approximate p-values because the matrix is
strongly structured; rank adjustment yields a more focused set of residual
condition-specific promoter responses.

![Approximate summary-level volcano diagnostics for the Kochanowski promoter-activity compendium. The panels show total effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-total-effect}, centered specific effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-specific-effect}, and rank-adjusted total effects $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},1}$. P-values are approximate calculations from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-approx-test} and are used here for exploratory ranking of processed reporter-condition summaries.](../../analysis/outputs/kochanowski_promoter_scaling/kochanowski_approx_volcano_three_targets.png){#fig-kochanowski-approx-volcano width="100%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

#### G.2 Analysis of an E. coli Fluorescence/OD Regulator-Stress Experiment {.unnumbered}

##### Screen Design and Response-Scale Calibration {.unnumbered}

We next reanalyzed the fluorescence reporter dataset of Dash et al.
[@Dash2024GlobalRegulators], which introduced an *E. coli* library of
global-regulator transcriptional reporters. GFP fluorescence and OD are
observed as matched time series. All available reporters contribute to
response-scale estimation, and downstream inference is restricted to the
weak-stress subset.

We consider four weak-stress reporters, Fur, MarA, SoxS, and LexA, measured
under excess iron, tetracycline, hydrogen peroxide, and kanamycin, with
standard growth as the reference condition. To avoid the initial reporter
ramp-up period, each time series is summarized over three post-ramp-up windows:
early, middle, and late. A reporter-window pair $\tilde a=(a,w)$ is used as the
analysis unit, where $a$ denotes the biological reporter and $w$ denotes the
time window. This
testing design contains 12 reporter-window units and four
non-reference stress conditions, yielding 48 reporter-window/stress contrasts.

For each retained well-window summary, let $F_i$ denote GFP AUC and let $O_i$
denote matched OD AUC in the same time window. We define the calibrated
fluorescence/OD response by the DStressR response equation,

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dryad-calibrated-response}
\widehat y_i
  =
  \log_2(F_i)
  -
  \widehat\alpha_{a_i}\log_2(O_i).
\end{equation}

Here the exponent is indexed by the biological reporter $a_i$, not by the
reporter-window pair. The time windows therefore act as repeated post-ramp-up
summaries for estimating a reporter-level growth-response relationship. We
estimate this response scale from the larger no-stress growth-transition panel,
which contains 18 reporters summarized over the same three windows. The
weak-stress inference then receives the four calibrated exponents for Fur,
MarA, SoxS, and LexA as supplied response-scale parameters.
In this run, the shrunken estimates were
$\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{Fur}}=-0.006$,
$\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{MarA}}=0.994$,
$\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{SoxS}}=0.251$, and
$\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{LexA}}=0.644$. Thus, response-scale estimation is
separated from the testing dataset: we use all suitable no-stress reporter data
to estimate growth correction, and then restrict differential testing to the
biologically targeted 12 by 4 weak-stress design.

##### Total, Specific, and Rank-1 Adjusted Effect Estimation {.unnumbered}

The total effect for reporter-window unit $\tilde a=(a,w)$ and stress condition $j$
is the reference-relative effect from Eq.\eqref{eq:total-effect}, evaluated
on the fluorescence/OD response scale in
Eq.\eqref{eq:dryad-calibrated-response}. This estimand asks whether the
reporter-window response changes under a stress condition relative to standard
growth. In this dataset, total-effect inference is closest to the biological
question addressed in the original weak-stress experiment: whether the reporter
library responds to the stress cues expected for the corresponding global
regulators.

We first inspect total effects on the calibrated fluorescence/OD response scale
(@fig-dryad-effect-decomposition, panel a). We observed a strong Fur response
under excess iron and additional Fur responses across other stresses. The other
canonical regulator-stress combinations also have positive total effects, but
they are weaker: MarA responds to tetracycline, SoxS to hydrogen peroxide, and
LexA to kanamycin.

![Effect decomposition in the *E. coli* fluorescence data. Rows are reporter-window units ordered by biological reporter and time window; columns are weak-stress conditions. The panels show the reference-relative total effect from Eq.\eqref{eq:total-effect} on the calibrated response in Eq.\eqref{eq:dryad-calibrated-response} (a), the default centered specific effect $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{spec}}$ (b), the estimated rank-1 component from Eq.\eqref{eq:low-rank-background-estimand} (c), and the rank-adjusted total effect $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot},1}$ (d). Black boxes mark the expected reporter-stress pairs across the three time windows in panels a, b, and d.](../../analysis/outputs/dryad_global_regulators/dryad_weak_stress_windows_calibrated_alpha_rank1_effect_decomposition.png){#fig-dryad-effect-decomposition width="100%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

We then compute the default DStressR specific effect by subtracting the stress-wide average response across the tested reporter-window units, $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{spec}}=\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot}}-\widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}}$, as in Eq.\eqref{eq:specific-effect}. The average is taken over the 12 tested reporter-window units. This
contrast answers a different question from the total effect: whether a
reporter-window response is unusually large or small relative to the average
response to the same stress condition. In the *E. coli* fluorescence data, the
specific-effect matrix highlights deviations from the stress-wide mean
response (@fig-dryad-effect-decomposition, panel b) and therefore emphasizes
reporter-window patterns around the stress-wide average.

To examine the effect of low-rank background adjustment, we use the
reporter-window by stress total-effect matrix from the *E. coli* fluorescence
data. The Fur-dominated response forms a structured mode across reporters, time
windows, and stresses. We therefore estimate one low-rank component from the
total-effect matrix
(@fig-dryad-effect-decomposition, panel c), and define a rank-adjusted total
effect before any optional centering step.

For the total-effect matrix
$T=\{\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot}}\}$, DStressR estimates the rank-1
background component described in
Eq.\eqref{eq:low-rank-background-estimand}. The rank-adjusted total-effect estimate is $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot},1}=\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot}}-\widehat B^{(1)}_{\tilde a j}$. We report the unadjusted total effects alongside the rank-adjusted total
effects (@fig-dryad-effect-decomposition, panel d), which ask what
reference-relative response remains after separating the dominant structured
mode. A rank diagnostic supports using a rank-1 adjustment in this dataset:
the first component explains 83.2% of the total-effect sum of squares, and its
singular value exceeds the 99% permutation reference. Biologically, this
component is dominated by the broad Fur response.

The Fur response defines a strong structured response mode in this small
matrix. For activation relative to standard growth, the total effects are the
relevant estimands. For weaker total reporter-window responses after separating
this dominant structured mode, the rank-adjusted total effect provides the
corresponding decomposition. Later-window MarA/tetracycline and LexA/kanamycin
effects become visible as positive residual signals, while the first low-rank
component captures most of the Fur/iron signal.

##### Inference Results {.unnumbered}

We next attach uncertainty to the three effect targets shown in @fig-dryad-effect-decomposition: total effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:total-effect}, default specific effects $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{spec}}$, and rank-adjusted total effects $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot},1}$ (@fig-dryad-three-target-inference). Across the 48 reporter-window/stress
contrasts, 36 total effects are significant after within-reporter
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. The default specific-effect analysis calls 42 of
48 contrasts. We interpret the many small p-values as evidence for a highly
structured effect matrix with broad shared signal across the tested
reporter-window units.

After rank-1 adjustment, the significant rank-adjusted total effects become
fewer and more selective. This inference result is consistent with the effect
decomposition in @fig-dryad-effect-decomposition: removing the dominant
structured Fur mode reduces broad stress-associated signal while retaining
several expected reporter-stress responses, especially later-window
MarA/tetracycline and LexA/kanamycin effects.

![P-value and volcano diagnostics for the three inferential targets in the *E. coli* fluorescence data. The top row shows raw p-value histograms and the bottom row shows the corresponding volcano plots for the same 48 reporter-window/stress tests. Total effects are the reference-relative responses from Eq.\eqref{eq:total-effect}; default specific effects are the centered contrasts $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{spec}}$; rank-adjusted total effects are the residual reference-relative responses $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot},1}$.](../../analysis/outputs/dryad_global_regulators/dryad_weak_stress_windows_calibrated_alpha_three_target_inference_combined.png){#fig-dryad-three-target-inference width="68%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="H"}

### Supplementary Note H: Scale of the Main and Supplementary Examples {.unnumbered}

Suppl. Table 5 summarizes the screen dimensions for the examples and
workflow reproductions discussed in the manuscript. Here $n$ denotes the
number of tested reporters, $p$ denotes the number of non-reference
perturbation levels, $M$ denotes the number of retained observations or
available summaries entering the analysis, and $|\Omega|$ denotes the number
of fitted or tested reporter-perturbation contrasts. The rows refer to the
Binsfeld, PFIbox, Campylobacter, Kochanowski, and Dash et al. datasets
[@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol; @French2018PFIbox; @Zannoni2026CampylobacterDrugScreen;
@Kochanowski2017PromoterScaling; @Dash2024GlobalRegulators].

```{r}

#| results: asis

  Example = c(
    "Binsfeld E. coli Lux/OD",

    "Campylobacter median-polish",
    "Kochanowski compendium",

  M = c("5,894", "228,977", "121,198", "1,600 summaries", "180"),
  Omega = c("658", "54,351", "57,349", "1,536", "48"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
names(scale_tbl)[7] <- "$|\\Omega|$"
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {

The Campylobacter row reports the reproduced pair-level median-polish workflow after filtering and replicate aggregation. The Salmonella empty-vector-control workflow in Supplementary Note B follows the same wide-screen geometry, with a small reporter panel measured across more than 2,000 perturbation/library-well levels.\\par\\smallskip\n")
  cat("\\centering\\scriptsize\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{3pt}\n")
}
cat(knitr::kable(
```
